opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The worry comes from the fact that the metric is really where our values get encoded into the system. When we train or select a model, we're optimizing toward some number, whether that's accuracy, F1, AUC, or a fairness criterion. That number implicitly says which mistakes matter and how much. If we pick it out of convenience or habit, because it's the default in a library or what the last paper used, we may be optimizing for something that doesn't reflect what we actually care about in the deployment setting.

Take a medical screening problem. A false negative and a false positive have very different costs, and those costs differ across contexts and stakeholders. Plain accuracy treats them as equivalent, so you can get a model that looks great on paper but behaves badly where it matters, especially under class imbalance, where predicting the majority class can look impressive.

The second issue is that the choice of metric isn't neutral with respect to model ranking. You can evaluate the same set of models under two reasonable-sounding metrics and get different orderings. So when a field converges on a leaderboard metric somewhat arbitrarily, it shapes which methods get published, which get adopted, and where research effort goes. We've seen this with large models, where some apparently "emergent" behaviors depend on choosing a discontinuous, all-or-nothing metric. Under a smoother metric the improvement looks gradual and predictable. The conclusion you draw about the science changes based on a measurement decision someone may not have thought hard about.

That's what motivates a lot of my work on metric elicitation. Instead of assuming the metric, can we learn it from the people who'll be affected, through comparisons or feedback, and then build systems that optimize the right trade-offs? Metrics are a design decision, and they deserve the same care we put into architectures and data.

r001.rationale: It says a metric chosen by convenience or habit may not reflect what matters in deployment, and can make a model look good while behaving badly where it matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. When we evaluate models, we're making a choice about what to measure, and that choice ends up defining what "better" means. And the thing that worries me is that in practice, those choices are often made pretty casually. Someone picks accuracy, or top-one accuracy on a particular benchmark, or some aggregate across a bunch of tasks, and then everything downstream, the leaderboard, the claims in the paper, the decisions about which model to deploy, all of that inherits the choice.

The problem is that different metrics can give you different answers. I've seen cases where you take the same set of models and the same set of benchmarks, and just by changing how you aggregate, whether you average raw scores or rank models per task and average the ranks, or normalize differently, the ordering of the models flips. And none of those choices is obviously wrong. They're all defensible. But if the conclusion depends on an arbitrary decision, then what are we actually learning? We're drawing conclusions that look very precise and very confident, and they're resting on something that was never really examined.

And I think it matters more now because evaluation has become so consequential. These numbers drive investment, they drive what gets deployed, they feed into policy conversations about which systems are safe or capable enough. So an arbitrary choice at the measurement stage isn't just an academic concern anymore. It propagates. If we're not careful about asking what the metric is supposed to capture, whether it actually captures that, and how robust our conclusions are to reasonable alternatives, then we're kind of building on sand. That's the part that worries me. Not that people are being dishonest, but that we've gotten comfortable treating these numbers as more meaningful than they've earned.

r001.rationale: The response says metrics can change model rankings and asks whether they capture what they are supposed to, but it does not clearly state that an arbitrary metric may fail to correlate with important real-world outcomes.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that the metric defines what we mean by success, but we often treat choosing it as an afterthought. We spend a lot of effort designing an algorithm and then evaluate it using whatever metric is standard for that benchmark, without asking whether that metric reflects the problem we actually care about.

Take a medical screening example. Accuracy treats a false positive and a false negative as equally costly. But missing a disease can have very different consequences from sending someone for an additional test. And if the disease is rare, you can get very high accuracy by predicting that nobody has it.

So these choices aren’t neutral. They encode tradeoffs, and changing the metric can change which model looks best. The concern is that we might make real technical progress toward a target that doesn’t capture what users need. We should be explicit about those tradeoffs and justify the evaluation criterion in terms of the application.

r001.rationale: The response says a standard metric may not reflect the problem people actually care about and can reward models that miss important outcomes, such as disease cases.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the metric is really a statement about what we care about. We often treat it as a technical detail—you pick accuracy or F1 because that’s what people have reported on that benchmark—but those choices can change which model looks best.

Take a medical screening problem. A false negative and a false positive can have very different consequences. Accuracy treats those errors equally, and if the condition is rare, you can get very high accuracy by predicting that nobody has it. So a good number doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve built a useful system.

What worries me is the disconnect between improving the metric and improving the outcome we actually want. We need to ask why a particular metric makes sense for the application, whose costs it captures, and what it might hide. Otherwise, we can put a lot of effort into optimizing something without knowing whether that improvement matters.

r001.rationale: The response says that improving a metric can be disconnected from improving the outcome people actually want, and gives screening accuracy as an example of a good score that may not indicate a useful system.
